name: 311 Service Requests
used_in: Status board, map, 311 charts, Open issues, community table, newsletter
method: A ward = requests whose comm_code is one of the ward's communities (the communities section of the dashboard lists them; a community belongs to the ward holding most of its area); Calgary = every request.
Requests in a period: requested_date from the first day of the first month to the last day of the last month. Duplicates are left out: status_description "Duplicate (Open)" and "Duplicate (Closed)".

Per 1,000 residents a year: requests in the area's residential communities / its residents at the middle of the period, counted the way chosen in Settings (the City's total shared by actual growth by default), x 1,000 x (12 / months in the period). Business areas have no residents, so their requests are in the totals but not in the rates.

Infrastructure reports: the 21 service types of the 311 study. Roads: Pothole Maintenance, Streetlight Maintenance, Traffic or Pedestrian Light Repair, Sidewalk - Curb and Gutter Repair, Roadway Maintenance, Backlane Maintenance, Debris on Street/Sidewalk/Boulevard, Signs - Missing - Damaged, Snow and Ice Control, Dead Animal Pick-Up, Pathway Concerns, Pathway Snow and Ice Concerns. Water (WATS): Catch Basin Concerns, Sewage Back-up, Sewer Maintenance, Water Main Break or Leak, Service and Main Valve Issues. Parks: Tree Concern - GIS, Garbage - GIS, Maintenance - GIS, Infrastructure - GIS.
Open requests: status_description exactly "Open" at the last refresh, whatever date they were made. Open more than 90 days: also requested_date more than 90 days before the refresh.

Closed within 7 days: requests made in the period with status "Closed" whose closed_date is within 7 days of requested_date, as a share of the period's requests closed so far (requests still open are not counted, so a short or recent period looks faster than it will end up). Calgary uses every request with a community.
Made through the app: source = "App" as a share of the period's non-duplicate requests (Web and Other, mostly phone, are the rest).
City service: the first part of service_name, before " - " (Roads, WATS = Water, WRS = Waste and Recycling, CT = Calgary Transit, Bylaw, Parks and so on).
The 311 study ("Who Calgary's 311 Hears"): requested_date 2024-10-01 to 2026-09-30, no duplicates, no blank community; it looked at nine northeast communities (56,473 requests).
excel: Filter comm_code to the area's community codes (see "Wards and their communities"), or to one community; for Calgary, no filter.
Filter requested_date between the first and last day of the months you want (dates sort as text: 2025-11-01).
Filter status_description: untick "Duplicate (Open)" and "Duplicate (Closed)". The row count is the number of requests.
For open requests: status_description = "Open" only, and no date filter.
cautions: Most requests are published at the community's centre point, not the exact address, so maps show 311 by community.

The City's own 311 ward dashboard counts by ward boundary from its internal system and is 1 to 3% higher; it also divides by 2021 Census households for every year, which favours large, fast-growing households.
"Closed" means the City closed the request, not always that the problem was fixed; some open requests are years old and may already be dealt with.

name: The City's printed ward profile (2021 Census)
publisher: City of Calgary (Statistics Canada 2021 Census, Community Data Program)
updated: 2021 Census (published 2023, revised July 2025); next: 2026 Census results from early 2027
used_in: Who lives here card, Data Genie reports
method: Figures are copied from the City's printed ward profile, the ward next to Calgary, and kept with the app (data/ward5_profile_2021.json, so far for one ward; every other ward uses "Who lives in each ward" below). Nothing is estimated or grown: they describe May 2021.
People in private households only; 2021 ward boundaries; income is for 2020; work questions refer to May 2021, during the pandemic.
excel: Open the ward's profile from the City's ward profiles page; each figure is in the table named on the card.
cautions: Calgary has about 14% more homes and about 21% more residents than in 2021 (much more in new communities), so shares today may differ.
Statistics Canada rounds counts to the nearest 5.

name: Being built (City projects, roads, large building permits)
updated: City projects: checked by hand (data/ward_projects.json); roads and permits: at each refresh
used_in: Growth vs amenities (Being built, Amenities), the dashboard amenities card, map layer, Data Genie
method: City projects under construction or approved that the City's open data lists of facilities do not have yet, each checked against the City's own project page.
Road projects: Road Construction Projects (sizs-hgef) in or near the area (all of Calgary for the city).
Large building permits: Building Permits (c2es-76ed) issued in the period in the area's communities, estimated project cost over $1,000,000 and no housing units, largest first.
excel: Building permits: filter c2es-76ed to the area's community codes, issueddate in the period, housingunits empty or 0, estprojectcost > 1000000; sort by estprojectcost.
cautions: Amenity counts include only facilities open now; a facility being built is listed separately until it opens.
Estimated project cost is what the applicant declared on the permit, not the final cost.

name: How residents are counted (Settings)
updated: Census: 2021; property roll: through the year; City outlook: each spring
used_in: Residents, every rate per 1,000, population charts, children estimates, newsletter, Data Genie
method: Four choices. The City's total, shared by actual growth, is the default (below). Growth model: each community's 2021 Census count grown with the homes on the property roll (see "Growth model" below).
2021 Census, no growth: each community's 2021 Census count (total_pop_household, f9wk-wej9), unchanged. The City's own 311 ward dashboard counts this way (it divides by 2021 Census households).

Grown to the City's total: all of Calgary adds up to the City's own population estimate for that month (Calgary and Region Economic Outlook 2026-2031, Spring 2026, Table 4 "City of Calgary Population Projection", page 19, Total Population as of April: estimates 2021-2025, forecast from 2026; November 2026 = 1,583,200 + 7/12 x (1,608,700 - 1,583,200) = 1,598,075). Communities built since 2021 have no 2021 count, so they keep their growth model count (19 communities, 29,547 people in November 2026). Every other community is its 2021 Census count x one factor = (the City's estimate - those new communities) / Calgary's 2021 Census count (1,288,995 people in private households). November 2026: (1,598,075 - 29,547) / 1,288,995 = 1.217, so each older community is 21.7% above its 2021 count. A ward is its communities added up.

The factor is more than growth: the City's estimate also counts people the 2021 Census count of private households leaves out (seniors' homes, residences, shelters) and those it missed. On Census day the City's estimate was already 2.7% above the Census count (1,323,783 against 1,288,995); the City's own growth from May 2021 to November 2026 is 20.7%. So "growth since 2021" under this choice reads higher than real growth, and growth for amenity flags always uses the growth model.

City's total, shared by actual growth: all of Calgary still adds up to the City's own estimate for that month, but growth is placed where homes were built. Each community = its 2021 Census count x f + the growth the growth model measured there (growth model count - 2021 count; for a community built since 2021, all of it). f = 1 + (the City's estimate - Calgary's growth model total) / Calgary's 2021 Census count. November 2026: 1 + (1,598,075 - 1,467,348) / 1,288,995 = 1.1014. So the City's growth the homes do not explain (more people per home since 2021, seniors' homes, residences, shelters, the Census undercount: 130,727 people) is spread over every community as a share of its 2021 count, and the growth from homes built stays where they were built. f is not people per home: it multiplies each community's 2021 count (+10.14% for every community). Going from the growth model, which already holds the 2021 count once, only the extra is added: residents = growth model + 2021 count x (f - 1). Calgary as a whole: 1,288,995 x 1.1014 + (1,467,348 - 1,288,995) = 1,598,075, the City's own estimate. A ward or community is worked out the same way from its own 2021 count and growth model count. Children: each community's 2021 children x one factor + the children the growth model adds for its new homes, the factor set so Calgary matches the City's forecast of children.
The largest community takes the person or two that rounding leaves over, so Calgary matches the City's figure exactly under both City's-total choices.

Every figure that uses residents (rates per 1,000, children, crowding at playgrounds and parks, Compare wards, property tax and budget per resident, the briefing screen) is worked out again under the choice; the website works all of them out under every choice each morning.
Rates per 1,000 residents = count / residents in the middle of the period x 1,000 x (12 / months).
excel: 2021 Census: filter f9wk-wej9 to the area's community codes and add up total_pop_household (all of Calgary's residential communities: 1,288,995).

City's total, shared by actual growth: f = 1 + (City's estimate - the growth model total over every residential community) / 1,288,995; each community = 2021 count x f + (growth model count - 2021 count).

Grown to the City's total: subtract the growth model residents of communities with no 2021 count from the City's population for the date, divide by 1,288,995 (f9wk-wej9 total_pop_household added up over every residential community), and multiply each older community's 2021 count by the result.
cautions: "Shared by actual growth" relies on the growth model's homes: where homes are missing from the property roll (some new towers until they are assessed), that community's growth is understated and every other community gets a little more of the factor.

The growth model follows homes built, so it can undercount established areas that grew by filling existing homes and towers (more people per unit); "grown to the City's total" grows every community at the same rate, so it undercounts communities where many homes were built.
The 2026 Census was taken in May 2026, but its counts are not published yet (population counts are due February 10, 2027); until then every choice is an estimate except the 2021 Census itself.
code: dashboard.py: POP_METHODS, DEFAULT_POP_METHOD, counts, _raw, actual_factor, city_factor, new_people, total_fix, estimate

name: Growth model (population today, every community)
updated: Property roll: through the year; Census: 2021
used_in: Residents today, every rate per 1,000, population charts, children estimates
method: Homes: accounts on the Current Year Property Assessments roll (4bsw-nn7w) with assessment_class = "RE" (residential), property_type = "LI" (land with a building) and sub_property_use starting with "R" (a dwelling: R110 single detached, R120 and R201 semi-detached and rowhouse, R401/R402 condominium units and so on).

Not homes, so left out: land-only lots (property_type "LO"), non-residential ("NR") and farmland ("FL") accounts, condo parking stalls (sub_property_use A004, addresses ending in V), storage units (A005, addresses ending in S) and other accessory or under-construction units (A000, A006, A007).
A home counts as lived in one year after its year_of_construction, spread evenly through that year, so homes built this year and part of last year are not counted yet.

A rental apartment building is one roll account; the model takes it out and adds its units instead (from matching building permits, data/rentals_all.json, every community in Calgary), at 2.0 people per unit or the community's 2021 household size if smaller.
People per home = (2021 Census population - people in rental units) / homes lived in on Census day (May 11, 2021). Residents = people per home x homes lived in + people per unit x rental units.

Where homes on Census day differ from 2021 Census households by more than 15% (24 communities across Calgary), new homes get the community's 2021 household size. Communities built since 2021 have no 2021 count, so they use the Calgary average (2.66 people per home).
2021 Census: 2021 Federal Census Population by Community (f9wk-wej9, total_pop_household) and Households (msjx-5ygv, total_private_households). Calgary: 1,288,995 people in 500,990 households.
excel: Download the roll for a community (4bsw-nn7w, comm_code = e.g. CNS).
Filter assessment_class = RE, property_type = LI, sub_property_use begins with R: that is the number of homes (Cornerstone, Oct 2026: 4,987).

Pivot year_of_construction against a count of roll_number to see homes by year built. The model then leaves out homes built in the last year or so and swaps rental buildings for their units (Cornerstone: 4,954).
cautions: An estimate, not a count: it holds 2021 people per home and does not count basement suites or more people moving into existing homes, nor people in seniors' homes, residences and shelters, so the Calgary total from the same method is 8.2% below the City's estimate (1,467,348 against 1,598,075, November 2026).
Tested against the City's 2016 and 2019 civic census: typical error about 3% by community, 6% for fast-growing ones. The 2026 Census by community (expected 2027) will allow a direct check.

name: Children (estimate)
used_in: Families and schools, child care spaces per 100 children, children per playground
method: Each community keeps its 2021 Census children (pop_age_0_to_4, pop_age_0_to_14) for the residents it had in 2021.

Residents added since 2021 are given the share of children seen in 2021 in the communities that were new at the Census, anywhere in Calgary: at least half of the homes lived in on Census day were first lived in during the five years before, and at least 500 residents. With the City's roll in November 2026 that is 12 communities, in every quadrant (Belmont, Carrington, Cityscape, Cornerstone, Greenwood/Greenbriar, Legacy, Livingston, Redstone, Seton, University District, Walden, Yorkville): about 24% aged 0 to 14 and 11% under 5. The list is worked out again at every update, so it can change; the current list and shares are in the dashboard data (population: new_share_communities, new_share_0_14, new_share_0_4). (Growth model.)

City's total shared by actual growth (the default): each community's 2021 children x one factor + the children the growth model adds for the homes built there; the factor is set so Calgary matches the City's forecast of children (dashboard.kid_factors_actual, kid_added, kids_as).

City's total, one rate for all: children follow the City's own forecast of children, from the same table as the population (Calgary and Region Economic Outlook 2026-2031, Table 4, page 19, Population by Cohort: 0-4, 5-9 and 10-14, as of April, read on a straight line between Aprils). Communities built since 2021 keep the estimate above; every other community is its 2021 count of children x one factor, so all of Calgary adds up to the City's forecast. November 2026: aged 0 to 14 = 270,400 + 7/12 x (273,300 - 270,400) = 272,092; aged 0 to 4 = 86,542.
excel: Share for new residents: add up pop_age_0_to_14 (and pop_age_0_to_4) of the communities above in f9wk-wej9 and divide by their total_pop_household. Then each community's 2021 Census children + (residents today - 2021 residents) x that share.
cautions: No public count of children by community exists after 2021.
The City's forecast is for all of Calgary, so each community keeps its 2021 share of the city's children under "grown to the City's total".
code: dashboard.py: CITY_KIDS_APRIL, city_children_at, kids_at, kid_factors, kid_added, kid_factors_actual, kids_as

name: Building Permits
used_in: Homes in building permits (status board, community table, newsletter)
method: Homes in permits = the sum of housingunits on building permits in the area's communities (communitycode).
"Applied for": applieddate in the period. "Issued": issueddate in the period.
excel: Filter communitycode to the area's community codes and issueddate (or applieddate) to the period; sum housingunits.
cautions: Planned homes, not finished ones: a home is lived in a year or more after its permit.

name: Development Permits
used_in: Development permit card, Growth vs amenities, newsletter
method: A ward = the permit's own ward field (e.g. "1" for Ward 1); Calgary = every permit. Applications = applieddate in the period.

Types are grouped from category: New homes and apartment buildings; Secondary (basement) suites; Change of use; New commercial and industrial; Non-residential renovations; Home businesses; Signs; Relaxations (small exceptions to the rules); Home additions and renovations; Other.
Larger developments = New homes and apartment buildings + Change of use + New commercial and industrial.
Approved = statuscurrent "Released". In review also counts "Approved" (decided, not yet released while the appeal period runs), Hold and Pending Appeal. Also counted: refused, cancelled.
excel: Filter ward to the ward's number (no filter for Calgary) and applieddate to the period; count rows, or group by category.
cautions: "Change of use" includes new child care centres, schools, clinics and places of worship.

name: Rezoning applications (land use redesignation, LOC numbers)
used_in: Growth vs amenities (Development and rezoning), map layer, Data Genie
method: Land Use Redesignation Applications (33vi-ew4s): applications to change a property's land use district (rezoning), often with an outline plan or road closure; numbers start with LOC. Council decides them at a public hearing.
The dataset has no ward or community, so each application is placed by its map point: inside the ward's boundary (Ward Boundaries, tz8z-hyaz) and in the community whose outline holds it.

Listed: every application with applieddate in the period, plus every one still open (status New, Submitted, Under Review or Miscellaneous) made since 2020, because a rezoning can take a year or more. "Rezoning applications" counts those made in the period; "still open" counts the open ones whenever made.
Proposed use = the current district (fromlud) to the proposed one (proposedlud), as the City writes them (for example R-CG to DC).
excel: Download 33vi-ew4s, filter applieddate to the period (or statuscurrent to the open ones) and keep the rows whose latitude and longitude fall in the area (a map check; the app tests the boundary exactly).
cautions: Public hearing dates are on Council agendas, not in the open data.
A large application can list several districts at once, separated by commas, in the same order.

name: Traffic Incidents
used_in: Traffic incidents (status board), map points
method: Incidents with start_dt_utc in the period whose exact latitude and longitude fall inside the ward's boundary (Ward Boundaries, tz8z-hyaz), or anywhere in Calgary for the whole city. The map shows the last 90 days of the period.
excel: Filter start_dt_utc to the period, then keep rows inside the ward (a map check; the app does the boundary test exactly).
cautions: The City stores times in UTC; the app converts them to Calgary time and counts months by Calgary dates. These are incidents the City reports for traffic, not every collision.

name: Community safety data (crime and disorder)
used_in: Crime tiles, Crime card, disorder card, Compare wards, newsletter, Data Genie
method: The spreadsheet linked as "Download Community Safety Data" on the police page; the app finds the current link at each refresh and downloads it only when it changes.
A ward = rows whose Ward column is that ward, e.g. "Ward 1" (the police assign each community to a ward, including the airport and business areas); Calgary = every row.
Crime categories: assault and other violence (not domestic), street and commercial robbery, break and enter (homes, businesses, other premises such as garages), theft from vehicles and vehicle theft.
The period is the dashboard period moved back to the latest month the police have published, compared with the same months a year before.

Per 1,000 residents a year: the ward's crimes / the ward's residents x 1,000 x (12 / months). Residents are counted at the middle month of the police period (for October to September, April), the way chosen in Settings. Calgary: all crimes in the file / every residential community's residents counted the same way, so the ward and Calgary are compared like with like. Under the default count (the City's total) Calgary's residents are the City's own estimate, so Calgary's rate is about 16.3 per 1,000 for Oct 2025 to Sep 2026; under the growth model, whose Calgary total is about 9% lower, it reads about 17.8.
Disorder: calls from the public about disorder (sheet "Disorder"), counted by event.
A few incidents in the file have no ward, so the 14 wards add up to slightly less than Calgary (Oct 2025 to Sep 2026: 25,857 crimes against 25,861).
excel: Download the spreadsheet: the "Police data file" button on the Crime card, or "Download Community Safety Data" on the police page. Sheet "Community Crime": filter Ward (e.g. "Ward 1"), or a Community, or nothing for Calgary; Year and Month; sum "Total Crime".

When someone asks for the source, open the police page at "Dashboard data download" (link above) and click "Download Community Safety Data": every crime number in the app can be found in that spreadsheet.
cautions: Totals in the app always match the police file.
The police leave out unfounded reports and domestic violence, and leave out incidents with no location; they advise against comparing the file directly with their dashboard.
Small communities swing a lot from year to year; compare with several years before quoting a change.
The police changed what counts as disorder in 2025, so older disorder years are not directly comparable, and a change against the year before can partly reflect the new definition.

name: Rental Market Survey (rents and vacancy)
updated: Yearly: surveyed each October, published in December or January
used_in: Rents and vacancy card, newsletter
method: CMHC surveys purpose-built rental apartments (buildings of 3 or more rental units) every October.

Read from the portal's Calgary tables: Average Rent, Vacancy Rate and Rental Universe, by bedroom count, for Calgary, each survey zone and each CMHC neighbourhood (see "Which CMHC rent area a ward gets").
Average rent is what sitting tenants pay, not the asking rent for empty units. Vacancy = units empty and ready to rent on the survey date.
excel: On the CMHC portal, open Calgary > Primary Rental Market > Average Rent > Neighbourhoods, and choose Export to Spreadsheet (CSV).
cautions: Condos rented out, basement suites and houses are not in the survey (CMHC's secondary market).
CMHC neighbourhoods and zones do not follow community or ward lines; no figures exist by community.
Letters are CMHC's reliability grades (a excellent to d use with caution); ** means not published.

name: Crime Severity Index
used_in: Crime in Calgary compared with other cities, newsletter
method: Overall, violent and non-violent index for the Calgary metropolitan area and other large cities, last 11 years, from Statistics Canada's Web Data Service.
excel: Download the table from the Statistics Canada page and filter Geography to Calgary, Alberta.
cautions: City level only. The index weighs each crime by how serious it is (100 = Canada in 2006); it is not a count and cannot be compared with the police ward counts.

name: Child Care Information
used_in: Families and schools, child care cards, newsletter
method: One file per quarter listing every licensed program, its type, licensed capacity and every inspection.
Programs are placed in a ward by their address (matched to the City's parcel addresses, 9zvu-p8uz).
Spaces = licensed capacity of programs located in the area. Family day home agencies are listed but not counted, because the homes they oversee are spread across the city.
Last 12 months: inspections (visits), non-compliance findings and enforcement actions (such as an order to remedy).
excel: Open the latest quarter's CSV, filter City = Calgary and the area's addresses or postal codes; sum Capacity once per program (the file has one row per inspection).
cautions: Capacity is how many children may attend at once, not how many are enrolled.

name: Student enrolment by school and Schools
publisher: Government of Alberta; City of Calgary
used_in: Schools cards, Families and schools, newsletter
method: School locations from the City's Schools dataset (fd9t-tdn2): schools inside the ward's boundary (every Calgary school for the whole city).

Each one is matched by name to the Government of Alberta enrolment file for each school year; students = the school's total enrolment (kindergarten to grade 12), split into K to 9 and grades 10 to 12.
excel: Open the Alberta enrolment file for a school year and filter School Name to the area's schools; sum Total.
cautions: Students are counted where they go to school, not where they live: many travel in from other wards and some of a ward's children go to school in another ward.

name: Amenities: recreation facilities, transit stops, playgrounds, community services
used_in: Amenities by community, map layers, Growth vs amenities
method: Each item is placed in a community by its location inside the community boundary (surr-xmvs).

Transit stops: status = ACTIVE. Playgrounds: playground equipment with life_cycle_status = ACTIVE and type_description = "MULTI PLAY COMPLEX" (one per play structure). Recreation facilities and community services (libraries, community centres) as listed.
Per 1,000 residents and children per playground use today's estimated residents and children.
excel: Download the dataset, filter the conditions above and count by community.
cautions: School playgrounds and private play areas are not City equipment and are not counted.

name: Road Construction Projects
used_in: Road construction card
method: Projects whose location is inside the ward or just outside it (all of Calgary for the whole city).
excel: Download the dataset and look for projects in or near the area.
cautions: Only the City's larger road projects; repairs and utility work are not listed.

name: Traffic Cameras
used_in: Traffic cameras, Briefing screen
method: Cameras inside the ward or within about 2 km of it (every camera for the whole city). The app saves each new image and replays the last 30 minutes.
cautions: The City keeps no recording; replays exist only while the app is open.

name: Buses and CTrains, live (Calgary Transit)
updated: Positions about every 30 seconds; timetable each service season
used_in: Map layer "Buses and CTrains, live"
method: Every 30 seconds while the layer is on, read Calgary Transit's vehicle positions feed (GTFS Realtime): each vehicle's fleet number, the trip it is running, where it is and which way it is heading.

Route number, route name and destination come from the trip, looked up in Calgary Transit's timetable (trips.txt and routes.txt in the GTFS file). A trip that is not in the timetable (an extra trip added on the day) takes its route number from the trip updates feed.
A vehicle with neither is shown grey as "Route not given": usually going to or from the garage.
The time shown is when Calgary Transit wrote the feed. Nothing is saved: the positions are read again each time.
cautions: Positions are where each vehicle last reported, not a prediction of where it is now.
The website reads the feed through the City's portal, which can pass it on a few minutes late; the time on the map says how old the positions are. The desktop app reads it directly.
The feed covers vehicles in service with a working locator; a few may be missing at any time.

name: Social Disorder Statistics (City open data)
used_in: Disorder card only when the police file is not available
method: Events in the area's community regions over the latest 12 months published.
cautions: No longer updated; the police community safety file replaces it.

name: Wards and their communities
used_in: Every ward view, Compare wards, City view
method: Ward outlines: Ward Boundaries (tz8z-hyaz), with each ward's councillor. Community outlines: Community District Boundaries (surr-xmvs), with each community's class (Residential, Industrial, Major Park ...) and sector.

Each community belongs to the one ward holding most of its area. The area is measured by laying a 24 x 24 grid of points over the community and counting how many fall in each ward; a sliver too thin for the grid goes to the ward holding its middle point.

Residential communities (class "Residential") have residents and per-resident rates; the others (industrial and business areas, major parks, undeveloped land) are listed and counted in totals but have no rates.
So every community is in exactly one ward and the 14 wards add up to Calgary.
excel: Open both datasets' maps on data.calgary.ca and lay one over the other; a community split by a ward line goes to the side with most of its area.
cautions: A community split between two wards is counted whole in one of them, so a ward's figures can differ slightly from figures the City or the police publish by exact ward line (the police assign each community to one ward too).

name: Rates per 1,000 residents, growth, and the "Growing" flag
used_in: Dashboard tiles, community table and map, Compare wards
method: Per 1,000 residents a year = count / residents x 1,000 x (12 / months in the period). For a 12-month period the last factor is 1.

Residents for a period are counted at its middle month (for November to October: about May), the way chosen in Settings (the City's total shared by actual growth, the default; the City's total at one rate for all; the growth model; or the 2021 Census). Open requests per 1,000 use today's residents.
A ward or city rate adds the counts of its residential communities and divides by their residents added together (not an average of community rates).
Communities with fewer than 100 residents get no rates ("too few residents for a rate"): one request would read as 10 or more per 1,000. Their requests still count in ward and city totals.

Growth since the 2021 Census = residents today / 2021 Census residents - 1. "Growing" marks communities that grew more than 30% (or did not exist in 2021). "New since 2021" means the 2021 Census counted nobody there.
Change against the year before = this period's count / the same months a year before - 1; counts are scaled to a year first when the two periods have different lengths.
excel: Take the count from the dataset with the same filters, divide by the residents shown for that community or ward, multiply by 1,000.
cautions: Rates depend on how residents are counted; the 2021 Census undercounts fast-growing areas, so their rates look higher than they are.

name: Compare wards: every measure
updated: With the whole-city view (at most hourly)
used_in: Compare wards, the city view's ward tables, Data Genie (section wards)
method: Every ward is built from the same whole-city data for the same period, so the 14 wards and Calgary line up.
Residents today, 2021 Census and children 0 to 14: added up over the ward's residential communities.

311 requests per 1,000 a year and infrastructure reports per 1,000 a year: requests (not duplicates) in the ward's residential communities / their residents at the middle of the period x 1,000. Infrastructure reports are the 21 service types of the 311 study.
Open requests per 1,000: requests still Open today in residential communities / residents today x 1,000.
Requests closed within 7 days: requests made in the period and Closed, with closed_date - requested_date of 7 days or less, as a share of all closed ones.
Requests made through the 311 app: share of the period's requests (not duplicates) with source = "App".

Crimes per 1,000 a year: the police count for the ward (the Ward column of the Community Safety Data file) / the ward's residents at the middle month of the police period x 1,000 x (12 / months). Calgary = all crimes in the file / every residential community's residents counted the same way, so ward and city rates compare like with like.
Change in crime and violent crime: the same months a year before.
Traffic incidents: each incident placed in a ward by its exact location (Traffic Incidents, 35ra-9556); per 1,000 uses the ward's residents at the middle of the period.
New homes: units in building permit applications for homes in the period (Building Permits, c2es-76ed); development permit applications: all types (6933-unw5).

Child care spaces per 100 children: licensed spaces in the ward's communities (Government of Alberta, family day home agencies not counted) / children aged 0 to 14 x 100; daycare and preschool per 100 children under 5 likewise. Schools and students: schools located in the ward and their latest enrolment.
Amenities: the share of homes within reach of each amenity and the crowding at playgrounds and parks (see "Growth vs amenities").

Rank "nth of 14": wards ordered best first where one direction is better (lower crime, faster closing, more amenities), otherwise highest first. Green or red: at least 10% better or worse than Calgary.
excel: Save the table with "Save this table"; every ward's figure can be rebuilt from the datasets listed, using the ward's communities (see "Wards and their communities").
cautions: 311 rates measure how much residents report, not how many problems there are: wards with more newcomers or fewer app users can report less for the same problems.

name: Growth vs amenities: how near homes are to amenities (distance from every home)
publisher: Calgary Data Desk (City of Calgary open data)
updated: Worked out again every week; the property roll every month
used_in: Growth vs amenities, Compare wards, Data Genie
method: Homes: every residential record on the City's property assessment roll (Current Year Property Assessments, 4bsw-nn7w, with assessment_class = RE, property_type = LI and a residential use code starting with R), each roll number once, placed at the mean of its parcel outline's corners. A purpose-built rental building is one record on the roll; it counts as its number of units (from a matching building permit, or estimated from assessed value).

Amenities, from the City's own inventory: playgrounds (Playground Equipment, bdu9-amk8, multi-play complexes that are active or installed), public parks (Parks Sites, kami-qbfh, every site except non-park and parks depot), transit stops (Calgary Transit Stops, muzh-c9qc, active), community centres and public libraries (Community Services, x34e-bcjz) and indoor recreation centres (Recreation Facilities, hxfu-6d96: leisure centres, aquatic and fitness centres and fieldhouses).

For every home and every kind: the straight-line distance in metres to the nearest one, in ANY community. Parks: to the nearest point of the park's edge (sampled every 20 m), 0 for a home inside a park.

Distances: playgrounds, parks and transit stops 400 m and 800 m; community centres 800 m and 1.6 km; recreation centres and libraries 2 km and 5 km. The 400 m for transit is the coverage distance in Calgary Transit's Service Guidelines (May 2025); every other distance is a choice, published at two distances so the effect of the choice shows.

For a community, a ward and Calgary, weighted by units: the share of homes within the first distance and within the second; the same for homes built since 2021 and homes built before 2021 (homes with no year are in neither); the median distance.

Reading for a community and an amenity, a stated rule, not a score: Too few homes (under 100 units); Measured gap (under half of units within the first distance); Check inventory (a measured gap where 25% or more of units were built in the last five years, because developer-built amenities may not be in the City's inventory yet); Most homes within reach (otherwise). Readings are never combined across amenities and there is no overall score.
excel: Take one community's homes from the property roll (4bsw-nn7w, the filters above) and the City's playgrounds (bdu9-amk8); for each home, the distance to the nearest playground = the smallest SQRT(((lon2 - lon1) x 69,880)^2 + ((lat2 - lat1) x 111,132)^2) metres; count the homes at 400 m or less and divide by all the homes.
cautions: Straight-line distance, not walking distance: walking routes are longer (curved streets, rivers, rail lines, major roads), so every share is the most generous reading.
The City's inventory only: school, developer, condominium, community association and private amenities are not counted.
A transit stop is not a service level: how often buses come is not measured.
The size and condition of amenities are not measured: each playground counts as one, whatever its size.
Rental units are partly estimated: purpose-built rental buildings count as their units, from building permits or, where no permit matches, estimated from assessed value.
New communities on the city's edge are naturally farther from shared facilities (recreation centres, libraries), some planned for later phases.
Community centre data needs checking: several large communities show no community centre within 800 m, which may mean community association halls are missing from the City's list.
code: access.py (compute, summarise, reading, shares, distances_to_points, distances_to_polygons)

name: Growth vs amenities: crowding at playgrounds and parks (two-step catchment, estimate)
publisher: Calgary Data Desk (City of Calgary open data)
updated: With every refresh (the population estimate changes monthly)
used_in: Growth vs amenities, Data Genie
method: Crowding asks how many people share the playgrounds and parks within reach. It is an estimate.

Children aged 0 to 14 and residents in each community come from the population model, counted the way chosen in Settings, and are spread evenly over the community's homes: children per unit = the community's children / its units.

Playgrounds, at 400 m and again at 800 m. Step 1, for each playground: the children of every home within the distance; its share = 1 / those children (a playground with no children within reach is skipped). Step 2, for each home: reach = 1,000 x the sum of the shares of the playgrounds within the distance (0 when none is).
A community, a ward or Calgary: the children-weighted average of reach over its homes, in playgrounds per 1,000 children.

Parks: the same, with each park's area in hectares in place of 1 and residents in place of children: hectares per 1,000 residents. A home is within reach of a park when it is within the distance of the park's edge.

Calgary's figure is simply the playgrounds with children within reach x 1,000 / the children in homes: the measure moves people between communities, it adds no playgrounds. The tab shows Calgary's figure under every way of counting residents, so the effect of the estimate shows.
No tier and no combining with distance: the crowding figure stands beside Calgary's, in its own column.
excel: Two playgrounds: 100 children live within 400 m of the first, 400 of the second, and no home reaches both. Shares: 1/100 and 1/400. A home near the first: 1,000 x 1/100 = 10 playgrounds per 1,000 children; near the second: 2.5. Calgary: (100 x 10 + 400 x 2.5) / 500 = 4 = 2 playgrounds x 1,000 / 500 children.
cautions: Children and residents are spread evenly over the homes of each community, from the population model's estimates (the 2021 Census plus modelled growth), not counted. The crowding figures will be firmed up with the 2026 Census age data in 2027.
Each playground counts as one, whatever its size; a park counts as its area.
Park crowding counts each park's whole area, natural areas and regional parks included, so homes near a very large park (Nose Hill, Fish Creek) show very high hectares per 1,000 residents.
Straight-line distance, the City's inventory only.

name: Growth vs amenities: amenity scores under every assumption (added 5 November 2026)
dataset: access (distance), access_crowding, population model (growth model and 2021 Census)
publisher: Calgary Data Desk (City of Calgary open data)
used_in: Growth vs amenities (scores), Data Genie
method: Crowding (two-step catchment, as for playgrounds and parks) for all six amenities: playgrounds per 1,000 children; park hectares per 1,000 residents; transit stops per 1,000 residents; community centres, indoor recreation centres and libraries per 100,000 residents. Each facility counts as one; a park as its hectares.
Amenity score = the community's crowding figure / Calgary's (1.00 = Calgary). Bands: under 0.50 well below; 0.50 to 0.80 below; 0.80 to under 1.25 around; 1.25 or more above.

Group scores, each amenity capped at 2.00 first: local = the mean of playground, park, transit stop and community centre (each within a walk); district = the mean of indoor recreation centre and library (each within a drive or a bus ride); all amenities = the mean of all six, with equal weights or with local amenities two thirds and district facilities one third. A group score needs every amenity in the group.

Every assumption: amenity and group scores are worked out 4 ways (each amenity's shorter and longer distance x two counts of residents: the one chosen in Settings and the 2021 Census); the all-six score 8 ways (x the two weightings). The figure shown is the shorter distance with the count chosen in Settings (and equal weights), with the range from the lowest to the highest. Changing the count in Settings changes every score.

"Near, but crowded" (playgrounds and parks, and any amenity in the table): most homes are within the first distance (the reading "Most homes within reach"), yet the amenity score is under 0.80: what is within reach is shared by more people than Calgary's average. Crowding counts everyone who can reach an amenity, from any community, so children from the next community who use the same playground share it too.
The local and district scores are the main figures. The all-six score is shown in each community's details only: one average of six different amenities can hide a gap in one group.

Labels: consistent gap = below 0.80 in every way with a figure; depends on assumptions = below 0.80 in some; no gap = never below. Communities with no 2021 Census count (built since) are scored fewer ways and marked.
A ward's score: its people-weighted crowding against Calgary's, worked out the same way. Communities with fewer than 100 homes are not scored.
excel: From the community details: score = crowding / Calgary's crowding; MIN(score, 2) for each amenity; local = AVERAGE of the three capped local scores; consistent gap when every one of the 4 (or 8) ways is below 0.80.
cautions: The comparison is with Calgary's own level, not a standard of adequate provision.
The 0.80 line and the bands are choices, applied the same way to every community.
Averaging unlike amenities (a transit stop, a library) is a choice too: the local and district scores are shown apart, and every amenity's own score is in the details.
A transit stop per resident is not a service level: dense areas with frequent buses can score low.
Community centre data needs checking (association halls may be missing from the City's list), which can lower district scores in newer communities.

Children and residents are spread evenly over the homes of each community, from the population model's estimates (the 2021 Census plus modelled growth), not counted. The crowding figures will be firmed up with the 2026 Census age data in 2027.

name: Elections: who represents each area, and the latest official results
dataset: Elections Calgary results file; gqvk-p23x; Elections Alberta Statement of Vote 2023 and official results; Elections Canada official voting results (45th general election); Legislative Assembly of Alberta; House of Commons; surr-xmvs
publisher: Elections Calgary (City of Calgary); Elections Alberta; Elections Canada; Legislative Assembly of Alberta; House of Commons; Government of Alberta (provincial boundaries)
updated: Read once a week; results change only with a new election, a by-election or a recount
used_in: Election Control Room (Control room, Know your leaders, Know your constituency, Full results), Dashboard (Who represents this area), Data Genie
method: Municipal, 20 October 2025: Elections Calgary's official results file (corrected after the 27 October 2025 mayoral recount): every candidate's votes for mayor, councillor in each ward, and public (CBE) and separate (CCSD) school trustee for each pair of wards. A share is a candidate's votes / the votes cast in that race. Calgary's turnout as Elections Calgary states it (voters / electors on the City of Calgary Permanent Electors Register). Elections Calgary does not publish turnout by ward. Three CCSD trustees were elected by acclamation.
Mayor by ward: the station-by-station results (gqvk-p23x) added up by ward for election-day stations; advance votes were cast at stations open to any ward, so they count for Calgary only.

Provincial, 29 May 2023: Elections Alberta's Statement of Vote, the "Total (All Voting Options)" row of each Calgary division (2019 boundaries, divisions 01 to 26): each candidate's votes, names on the list, ballots cast (valid + declined + rejected) and turnout (ballots / names on the list). By-elections since in Calgary divisions (Calgary-Shaw, 14 September 2026) from Elections Alberta's official results, read the same way. The member sitting today from the Legislative Assembly of Alberta's member list.
Referendum, 19 October 2026: Elections Alberta's official results by electoral division for each of the 10 questions; Calgary = its 26 divisions added up.

Federal, 28 April 2025: Elections Canada's official voting results, tables 11 (electors, ballots, turnout) and 12 (candidates and votes) for Calgary's 11 districts; the members sitting today from the House of Commons.

Who represents a ward: a ward and a provincial electoral division or federal electoral district have different borders. Each community's area is split over the divisions and districts (a grid of points inside its outline; shares under 1% left out), and a ward's share in one = its communities' residents x their shares / its residents (the count chosen in Settings). The councillor and school trustees follow the ward.

Seats: Calgary City Council (the mayor and 14 councillors by local political party, independents together), Calgary's MLAs and MPs by the caucus of the member sitting today, and the whole Legislative Assembly (87 seats) and House of Commons (343 seats) from their member lists; a seat with no sitting member is vacant. Each party keeps one colour across the charts; they are not the parties' own colours.

Know your constituency (a ward): electors are estimated, as Elections Calgary does not publish electors by ward: each community's residents x the share of residents on the federal electors list in its electoral district (Elections Canada 2025: electors / 2021 Census population), scaled so Calgary adds up to the City's electors register (896,042). Estimated turnout = votes cast in the ward's councillor race / estimated electors. The ward's provincial and federal turnout and its referendum shares average its electoral divisions or districts by the share of its residents in each. The councillor race station by station is from the station results (gqvk-p23x). Who lives here: the City's ward profile (2021 Census); what residents raise: open 311 requests.

Nothing is ranked, scored or recommended: results are shown as published, candidates in order of votes. The insights are facts worked out the same way for every race, for any candidate or campaign alike.
excel: Municipal: the open data table gqvk-p23x; filter officecategory = Mayor and ward = the ward number to add up a ward's election-day votes.
Provincial: the Statement of Vote workbook, sheet = the division number, row "Total (All Voting Options)".
cautions: Ward electors and turnout are estimates (see the method); the City's register and the federal list differ, and people move.
Shares of a ward in each electoral division or district are by area within each community, not by where each home is: a community split by a boundary is split by area.
Alberta's electoral boundaries are being redrawn for the general election on 18 October 2027; the divisions here are those of the 2023 election.
Elections Calgary notes that its station-by-station results do not include special (mail-in) ballots.

name: What changed on 5 November 2026 (Growth vs amenities)
used_in: Growth vs amenities (What changed)
method: The earlier method, removed: Counted City assets inside each community's boundary (benches, picnic tables, playgrounds, sports equipment, fitness equipment, bins, off-leash areas, neighbourhood park space, trees, transit stops) per 1,000 residents (playgrounds per 1,000 children). Divided each by Calgary's figure, capped each at 2.00 and averaged them into an "amenity level" (1.00 = the city). Flagged communities that grew more than 20% since 2021 (or were new) and sat below 0.75: 23 communities on 5 November 2026. A "Needs attention" tab ranked communities Urgent, High or Watch with a growth weight (0.5 + growth % / 200) and listed what each would take to reach the Calgary level.

Why: an audit on 5 November 2026 found that counting inside the boundary per resident misled. A playground across the street in the next community counted as zero: North Haven Upper had no playground inside its boundary, yet 96% of its homes are within 400 m of one. Across about 215 communities the rank agreement between the two measures was about 0.45.

The method now: the distance from every home to the nearest amenity, in any community (see "Growth vs amenities: how near homes are to amenities"), and for playgrounds and parks how many children or residents share the ones within reach (see "crowding").

Removed with it: the amenity level, the Needs attention tab and its Urgent, High and Watch tiers, the growth weight, the "what it would take" list and per-resident amenity counts as headline figures. The earlier list of 23 communities is replaced.

name: Homes: how they are counted (each ward, each community)
dataset: 4bsw-nn7w (Current Year Property Assessments), msjx-5ygv (2021 Census households)
used_in: Compare wards (Homes), Growth vs amenities (growth checks), community details, the growth model
method: Start from every account on the City's property assessment roll.
Keep the residential class only (assessment_class RE): commercial and industrial property (NR) and farm land (FL) are left out.
Keep land with a building only (property_type LI): vacant lots and land without a building (LO) are left out.

Keep residential uses only (sub_property_use starting with R): detached houses (R110), semi-detached and duplex homes (R120, R121), condo apartments in low-rise (R201, R202) and high-rise buildings (R301, R302), townhouse and row units (R401, R402) and the other R codes. Condo parking stalls (A004, about 59,000 accounts, e.g. "60V 9449 19 ST SW", $10,000), storage lockers (A005, e.g. "119S") and other non-home accounts (A codes) are separate accounts on the roll and are left out, so a condo with a stall and a locker counts once.
Each home counts as lived in one year after its year of construction (homes added evenly through each year).

Rental apartment buildings are one account for the whole building: the building is taken out and its units are added from matching building permits (lived in 6 months after the permit is completed) or, where there is none, estimated from its assessed value.
Homes on Census day are checked against the households the 2021 Census counted: Calgary 494,282 homes against 500,990 households (1.3% fewer); each ward's check is on Growth vs amenities.
A ward's homes are the homes of its communities (the ward holding most of each community's area). Residents per home = residents (the way chosen in Settings) / homes lived in today.
excel: Download 4bsw-nn7w filtered to assessment_class = RE, property_type = LI and sub_property_use starting with R, for the community codes of the ward; count the rows by year_of_construction.
cautions: Homes, not people: a home holds more people where households are larger, and secondary suites in houses are not separate accounts, so a house with a basement suite counts as one home.
Residents per home is a check on the way of counting: Ward 10 shows 3.82 under "one rate for all" on only 1.7% more homes since 2021, a sign that one rate for all overstates it.
code: population.py: HOMES_WHERE, homes, units, homes_lived_in, recon; dashboard.py: ward_summaries, population_recon. Growth vs amenities > Population build-up shows it community by community and lists every property

name: Growth checks: is the population growth believable?
dataset: 4bsw-nn7w (homes), City population outlook, Alberta student enrolment by school, fd9t-tdn2 (schools)
publisher: City of Calgary; Government of Alberta
used_in: Growth vs amenities (top), Data Genie
method: Homes alone: homes lived in on the property roll today / at the 2021 Census - 1, people per home as in 2021 (close to the growth model, which uses each community's own people per home).

Homes plus more people per home: Calgary's people per home change = (the City's estimate now / at the Census) / (Calgary's homes now / at the Census) - 1, about +5.5% (20.7% more people on 14.4% more homes). The area: (1 + its homes growth) x (1 + that change) - 1 = real growth. For all of Calgary this gives the City's own growth: 1.144 x 1.055 = +20.7%. Read against the 2021 Census count, like the ways of counting that add up to the City's total, it is x 1.027 (the City's estimate on Census day / the Census count: people the Census count of private homes left out).
School enrolment: students in the area's schools from 2021/2022 to the latest year, against every Calgary school; Calgary's growth x (the area's enrolment growth / Calgary's).

The range runs from the lowest to the highest check; each way of counting is marked within it, within 1 point of it (rounding and the growth model's own people per home in each community), or above or below it.
excel: Homes: sum homes_now and homes_census over the area's communities (the dashboard's community table).
cautions: Each check assumes something: that homes filled up like Calgary's average, or that children moved with the population. Schools take students from outside the area, and a new school pulls students in.
The 2026 Census (counted May 2026) settles it: population counts are released on February 10, 2027.

name: Live population counter (dashboard)
updated: Every second in the browser; its two anchor figures every refresh
used_in: Dashboard (Residents today tile)
method: Work out the selected area's residents on the first day of this month and of next month, the way of counting chosen in Settings (the same calculation as every other figure).

Join them with a straight line: residents now = this month's figure + (next month's - this month's) x (time since midnight on the 1st) / (time from the 1st to the 1st of next month), shown to 3 decimals.

Under the City's total the monthly figures sit on the City's straight line between April figures, so the counter moves at the City's forecast pace: from April 2026 to April 2027, 1,583,200 to 1,608,700, about 70 people a day for Calgary. A ward moves at its own pace under the chosen count.

Each morning's refresh works the two figures out again and the counter carries on from there; at the end of the month the next line starts exactly where this one ends. Under the 2021 Census count it stands still.
excel: (Next month's figure - this month's) / days in the month = people a day; this month's figure + people a day x days since the 1st = today's live figure.
cautions: A forecast pace, not a count: nobody counts residents day by day.
code: dashboard.py: population_live, _local_midnight_ms (the browser draws the same straight line, ui/app.js livePop)

name: Amenities that are not the City's (OpenStreetMap), without double counting
dataset: OpenStreetMap: leisure=playground, fitness_station, pitch (sport=basketball), dog_park, park
updated: Read again every week with the City's assets
used_in: Growth vs amenities (the optional "Count private amenities" filter, playgrounds and parks), Assets list
method: Ask OpenStreetMap (Overpass API) for every playground, fitness station, basketball court, dog park and park inside a box around Calgary.

Take out every one the City already lists: a City playground (Playground Equipment) within 80 m of its middle or inside its outline; City fitness equipment or a basketball hoop (Parks Sport Equipment) within 40 m or inside it; a dog park whose middle is inside a City off-leash area or within 100 m of one's middle; a park with 30% or more of its area inside City park sites (Parks Sites). Anything tagged as operated or owned by the City of Calgary is the City's too.

Take out closed, customers-only, paid and indoor ones. Ones marked private (residents only: homeowners' association, condo) are kept apart and count only when the "include private ones" filter is on (off by default); they still take part in the duplicate check. Also take out the same thing mapped twice (within 25 m or inside an outline already counted; parks 30% inside one already counted), and parks under 0.05 ha or over 20 ha.

Place each one left in the community holding its middle and count it: playgrounds, fitness stations and dog parks 1 each; basketball courts their hoops tag (else 1); parks their area in hectares, added to neighbourhood park space.

They are listed beside the City's counts in the Assets list. On Growth vs amenities they count only when the "Count private amenities accessible to the community" filter is on (off by default), and then only for playgrounds and parks: the distance to the nearest one and the crowding. An OpenStreetMap park is a circle of its own area around its middle. Gated, residents-only ones count only when "Also count gated" is ticked too.
excel: Open overpass-turbo.eu, run the query for one kind (for example leisure=playground) over a community, and compare each result with the City's Playground Equipment points (bdu9-amk8) on the same map.
cautions: Volunteer-edited: coverage is uneven; a missing feature means nobody has mapped it yet.
Matching is by distance: two separate playgrounds closer than 80 m count as one City one.
A fitness station may hold several pieces, the City counts each piece.
code: osm.py (fetch, build, MATCH_M, PARK_OVERLAP, SAME_M); assets.py builds both counts; dashboard.with_other

name: Map shading, flags and colours
used_in: Maps, Compare wards, tiles
method: A ward map shades its communities in 5 equal steps from the lowest to the highest value.
The whole-city map has about 200 communities, so it uses 5 equal-sized groups instead (each shade holds a fifth of the communities), so a few extreme values do not wash out the rest.
Compare wards map: 5 equal steps between the lowest and highest ward; where one direction is better the darker shade is always the better one.
Change chips are green or red only where a direction is clearly better (crime down is good); counts of 311 reports are shown neutral, because more reporting is not in itself good or bad.

name: Who lives in each ward (2021 Census by ward)
used_in: Who lives here (every ward), Compare wards, Data Genie
method: Population and Dwellings by Ward (k4pr-cznc), Families and Households by Ward (jzfi-qvb4) and Employment by Ward (b5q8-82zn), against the same three tables for the whole city (fm6w-acnx, u75s-8rqc, 8w7b-2yqx).

Shares: children 0 to 14 and seniors 65+ / people in private households; households of 5 or more and people living alone / private households; one-parent families / census families; in the labour force / people 15+; unemployed and self-employed / the labour force.
One ward also shows the City's printed ward profile (languages, newcomers, housing costs, income), kept with the app (see "The City's printed ward profile").
excel: Download the three ward tables and divide the columns named above.
cautions: 2021 Census on the wards as they were in 2021; the 2026 Census replaces it when the City publishes it.

name: Which CMHC rent area a ward gets
used_in: Rents and vacancy, newsletter
method: A CMHC neighbourhood is used when its name lists at least a quarter of the ward's residential communities (and at least two); otherwise the CMHC survey zone matching most of the ward's communities' sectors (Northeast, Northwest ...) is shown and named as a zone. The city view shows Calgary only.
cautions: CMHC areas do not follow ward lines.

name: City budget
used_in: City budget, Data Genie
method: Every line of Calgary Open Budget, added up by year, budget (operating or capital), department and business unit. Operating is "Operating Expenditures Net of Recoveries"; capital is "Capital". Amounts are in millions of dollars, as the City publishes them.
Per resident = the budget / the City's population estimate for this month.

By ward: the City does not publish its budget by ward. The ward table adds up only the published costs of City and partner projects and road projects listed in the app with a location in the ward (the largest dollar amount named in each project's cost).
excel: Download fqax-i3nz, filter year and fund, and sum budget by budget_department.
cautions: Project costs are often spread over several years and shared with other governments, so they do not add up to a year's capital budget.

name: Property tax by ward and community (estimate)
publisher: City of Calgary; Alberta Municipal Affairs (bylaw)
updated: Roll: through the year, read weekly; rates: each spring (bylaw)
used_in: City budget (property tax by ward), Data Genie
method: The City does not publish property tax by ward. Assessed values: the Current Year Property Assessments roll (4bsw-nn7w), added up by community and sub_property_use, for residential (re_assessed_value), non-residential (nr_assessed_value) and farm land (fl_assessed_value).

Exempt property left out: non-residential property whose sub_property_use starts with S (public and institutional: hospitals, schools, universities, places of worship, utilities, police and fire, airport) or P (parks, reserves, libraries, arenas, pools, museums).

Scaling: what is left is multiplied, class by class, so Calgary's total equals the taxable assessment in the bylaw (municipal: residential x 0.9765, non-residential x 0.7885). Exemptions the roll does not show are spread evenly.

Tax billed = scaled assessment x the bylaw's rates. 2026 municipal (City) rates: residential 0.0038906, non-residential 0.0179986, farm land 0.0339557; education (Province): residential 0.0027593, non-residential 0.0041502, farm land 0.0027593.

City share = the municipal tax; the rest of the bill is the Province's education tax, which the City collects and passes to the Government of Alberta. Paid on homes = residential tax / all tax billed.
A ward is the sum of its communities (the City's community-to-ward table). Calgary's total equals the bylaw's levy: $3,756.6M ($2,520.9M City, $1,235.7M education).

Against the budget: the 2026 budget book's "Property tax, including levies" ($2,551M) also holds local improvement and community revitalization levies and tax from properties added during the year, which cannot be placed by ward; the City share placed in wards is $2,521M.
excel: Download 4bsw-nn7w with comm_code, sub_property_use, re/nr/fl_assessed_value; drop rows with nr value and sub_property_use starting S or P; sum by community; multiply by the factors and rates above.
cautions: An estimate of tax billed (the levy), not tax collected: arrears, appeals and in-year changes are not published by property.
Exempt business property the roll does not flag is spread evenly, so wards with much public or institutional land (Ward 7 downtown, industrial wards 9 and 10) carry the most uncertainty.

name: Report auditor (Data Scientist)
dataset: The report and the queries behind it
used_in: Data Scientist, Report auditor tab
method: Step 1, audit by Chinook: reads the report and every query it ran, re-runs the queries with the same filters and periods, recomputes every total, rate, share and change with the calculator, and checks the sources, the method, the wording and the recommendations. It lists findings with its evidence and changes nothing.

Step 2, review and fix by Bow: re-checks each finding itself, accepts, revises or rejects it with its own numbers and reasons, and makes the corrected report, changing only what the accepted and revised findings require.
Step 3, final check by Rundle: checks only the step 1 findings: each accepted one fixed correctly in the corrected report, each rejected one rightly rejected.
The audit page lists every finding with all three verdicts; the corrected report is saved like any report (title ending "(audited)").
excel: Each finding names the query or calculation re-run, so it can be repeated by hand.
cautions: The engines can still miss a problem; a finding the final check marks "not fixed" or "wrongly rejected" needs a person to look at it.
Reports made before the auditor existed are checked from their text, without the list of queries behind them.

name: Daily climate data, Calgary International Airport
used_in: Data Genie
method: Daily temperature, rain, snow and snow on ground at the Calgary International Airport station (northeast Calgary), back to 1881; grouped by month or year on request. The forecast is Environment Canada's public forecast for Calgary, about 7 days ahead.
cautions: One station for the whole city: snow and temperature vary across Calgary.
